newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Some Russian gas group assets frozen for back tax.
newsitem.headline: Some Russian gas group assets frozen for back tax.

text.p: The Russian government, scrambling for cash, has frozen some assets of gas monopoly RAO Gazprom in a desperate attempt to rake in $2.8 billion in unpaid taxes.

Rem Vyakhirev, chairman of the company, said the government was taking inventory and had frozen the accounts of Gazprom's major production unit, which accounted for almost half of its 560 billion cubic metre (19.8 trillion cu ft) gas production last year.
"This attempt to collect taxes...will bring massive bankruptcy and dooms us to collapse," Vyakhirev said in a letter to parliament.

Unpaid taxes are one of the biggest problems facing the government, which is struggling to meet the terms of a $10 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund. Russia collected only 60 percent of planned taxes in the first half of the year.
Gazprom, Russia's largest company and a freewheeling spender, is an obvious target.
Gazprom admits it owes more than 15 trillion roubles ($2.8 billion) of taxes but says it is owed more than three times that amount by consumers, which include the government.

The company, where Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and Energy Minister Pyotr Rodionov both once worked, has been viewed as a state within a state and many analysts question whether the government has the will to take the powerful company on.
It is also rich. "It's hard to believe those guys aren't falling all over money," said one Western economist.

But Gazprom said its troubles stemmed from non-payment by customers including the government. "We supplied gas for which the government did not pay and then we are asked for taxes on money we did not receive," Vyakhirev said.

Economists said the quarrel might be sorted out by netting out debts -- forgiving both taxes for unpaid bills and unpaid bills between firms which make a vicious tangle of financial rope strangling Russia's economy.

"But at the end of the day that does not solve anything -- real income must be generated for the budget," said United City Bank chief economist Christopher Granville, who predicted that Russia and Gazprom would reach a compromise cash settlement.

World Bank chief economist Vladimir Konovalov said the government meant business and that real change would have to happen. "The government is screaming for money. This is not a game," he said, adding that the move was a welcome surprise.

"The energy sector has not been paying its fair contribution to the government... The whole natural monopoly area of Russia needs to be looked at," he said, suggesting that the government consider demonopolising parts of the company.

But some analysts said the move's awkward timing, days before Gazprom is due to announce the terms of an international equity placement, suggested the government had made an uncoordinated move rather than a lightning strike.
"It could be a case of the right hand not knowing what the left hand is doing," said MC Securities gas analyst Stephen O'Sullivan.
